headline: Highest risk is ECC’s filesystem/MCP write surface interacting with langchain4j-based workflows, creating medium prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure; no direct evidence of a shared channel or compliance mismatch.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC can read/write the filesystem, use MCP, and process files and hooks; if langchain4j is wired to consume ECC-produced content or shared files, attacker-controlled text could be treated as instructions. The pair lacks direct documentation of a shared channel, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF both agents share a filesystem, clipboard, or MCP endpoint
IF langchain4j ingests ECC output as trusted instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable shared MCP endpoints for the pair
Separate working directories and temp paths
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent files
Require explicit allowlists for instruction-bearing content
requires-engineering: add parser hardening and content-sanitization gates

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC touches session summaries, learned skills, hooks, git history, and security findings, while langchain4j is a framework that may be configured to move data through application code. Because the pairwise data flow is undocumented, leakage is plausible in default integrations and uncertainty warrants medium rather than low.
conditions: IF ECC files or session artifacts are mounted into a langchain4j application
IF the application forwards those artifacts to an external model or service
mitigations: Keep ECC artifacts out of shared mounts
Restrict file permissions on session and hook directories
Review outbound destinations in the langchain4j app
Rotate any exposed secrets in ECC-managed files
requires-engineering: implement data-loss-prevention filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, and network egress, while langchain4j is commonly embedded in apps that may also mutate shared resources. No locking or coordination is documented, so overlapping writes to the same workspace or git state are plausible and can corrupt work products.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or git repository
IF the surrounding orchestrator does not provide locks or serialization
mitigations: Assign separate repositories or worktrees
Pause one agent during the other's write phase
Use file locks around shared outputs
Review git status before each write step
requires-engineering: add optimistic-concurrency controls

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC can generate and store security findings, documentation, and session summaries; if langchain4j consumes those outputs as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream actions or responses. The pair lacks evidence of verification gates, so the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF langchain4j uses ECC-generated text as a source of truth
IF no human or automated verification step checks ECC outputs before reuse
mitigations: Require review before reusing ECC outputs
Mark ECC outputs as untrusted by default
Add checksum or provenance metadata
Limit downstream actions to read-only previews
requires-engineering: insert validation and approval gates

E_compliance.rationale: ECC handles session and security-related data with configurable retention and local file surfaces, while langchain4j exposes no explicit residency or retention commitments in the profile. No concrete mismatch is documented, so only a low compliance risk is supportable from the profiles alone.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in ECC session files
IF the deployment of langchain4j has stricter retention or residency rules than ECC
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in ECC sessions
Set short retention on ECC artifacts
Document the data classes allowed in the pair
Review deployment residency settings
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion workflows
